title: Map Contains and Remove
story: Your app tracks user sessions. When a user logs out, you need to delete their session from the Map. But first, you check: are they even logged in? You need to ask 'does this key exist?' before trying to remove it.
why: `.contains()` answers 'is this key present?' and `.remove()` deletes entries — essential for managing dynamic key-value data.
analogy: `.contains()` is like asking a librarian 'Do you have this book?' — a simple yes/no. `.remove()` is like checking out a book — you take it off the shelf AND get the book itself. If the book isn't there, the librarian says 'Sorry, we don't have that one' (None).
try_it: Build a simple LRU (Least Recently Used) cache: when the cache is full (say 3 items), remove the oldest entry before inserting a new one. Use `.contains()` to check cache hits. Add a `touch` function that 'refreshes' a key by removing and re-inserting it — this moves it to the 'most recently used' position.
tips: Use `.contains()` for yes/no checks — it returns Bool, cleaner than `.get()` when you don't need the value
`.remove()` does two things: deletes the entry AND returns the old value — like popping from a Vec but by key
Call `.contains()` before `.remove()` if you want to avoid the Option — but matching on remove is often cleaner
common_mistakes: Using `.get()` just to check existence — `.get()` requires matching on Option; `.contains()` gives a clean Bool
Forgetting that `.remove()` returns `Option[V]` — if the key wasn't there, you get None, not a crash
Expecting `.remove()` to keep the old value accessible — once removed, the data is gone from the Map
